translations.text: Saint Hippolytus's discourse on the blessings of Jacob, how he blessed the twelve patriarchs.
Words to expound the blessings of Jacob.
I seek those blessings from the Lord, for who among men is able to expound the spiritual books, unless that supernal wisdom is his helper in the task?
Or who is able to expound the written words of the blessed prophets, left unrevealed in parable?
Unless the Word himself expounds them, as in former times in Israel,
when, like a lamp, he was hidden in the Law under a bushel, so that he might be able to enlighten those justified by the Law through circumcision.
And now he is openly upon the wood, as on a lampstand, the seven-faced lamps lit and displayed, so that by his own lamp he may call even the distant peoples to life.
For those things were only as a type. Jacob and Rachel were not the sun and the moon.
Nor did this come to pass in that way, for Rachel had long since been lying buried by that road.
And Joseph, when he met his father, was the first to bow down to him, so that the type might stand and the Scriptures be found justified.
Now where then is that saying fulfilled: "Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come and bow down to you?"
Rather, it was when the twelve blessed apostles, with Joseph and Mary, went up to the Mount of Olives and worshipped Christ,
for Judas was not with them, nor was Joseph himself Christ, that this should be reckoned as having happened in Egypt.
Rather, it resembled the types of things to come, which were revealed beforehand through Joseph.
Let that true and heavenly interpreter now be set forth in our midst, for what was proclaimed by him to the blessed prophets, let him likewise reveal a second time!
Yet the Scriptures did not turn aside from Joseph, so as not to call him an interpreter, for he was the one who recounted the counsels hidden concerning the Father.
And the Scriptures say that they did not know that Joseph understood them, for an interpreter stood between them.
What profit was it then for those brothers to slaughter the kid, so as to deceive their own father?
Behold, now Joseph is alive in Egypt. Why did you falsely defile that flowered garment with blood,
as you did, so that father Jacob recognized that garment and accepted from you that it had happened?
You sell Joseph, O Judah, overcome by the desire of this world, and they sold him to those foreign Ishmaelites,
so that he might go down to Egypt and there be given over to prison, and dreams be revealed by him, so that he might be sought out by Pharaoh and appear as king of the Egyptians.
And afterward he would appear as a faithful steward, and wheat would be gathered by him in abundance and stored in the treasuries,
and the seven years would be completed, and the people would be nourished through the famine, and he would receive worship from his brothers and be called lord by them.
Now how should I not glorify the King of the heavens, who has shown us his own counsels through the prophets, as if seen in a mirror?
But since this occasion demands an explanation of the blessings, let us attend to them with diligence of mind,
so that those blessings spoken by Jacob may, as blessings, be fulfilled upon the sons of Israel. But I also find there what came to pass [?]:
those blessings were suited to the sons themselves, and a great prophecy was shown forth through them, which was fulfilled upon the children to come, for the confirmation of his race.
And if this is so, then blessed Jacob was speaking to his sons in accordance with those times.
But the things he said became manifest after many ages, and he was performing and bestowing those blessings for the sake of that which he was foretelling.
But to the sons of Israel he spoke about their sins, fittingly for each of them, and he separated himself from such deeds of theirs.
We find the same pattern with blessed Isaac, who blessed Jacob, his younger son, and granted everything to him, because Christ was destined to be born from him in the flesh.
And concerning Esau he knew beforehand that he would bear the figure of that people.
And he perceived the wicked intent of his heart and did not bless him, but condemned him by the power of his words.
And that this is so can be clearly understood from the Scriptures, from what follows,
for it speaks thus: When Isaac called his firstborn son and said to him: "Take your bow and quiver and go out to the field and hunt game for me and make me food,
such as I love, and bring it to me, and I will eat, and my soul will bless you while I am still alive."
And what the prophet commanded Esau, when he asked food from him, signifies in word the showing forth of that first people,
which was seeking the fruit of righteousness by means of that which was reckoned as spiritual food.
And when he said, "Go out to the field and hunt for me," he signifies to us the figure of walking in the way of this world, after the manner of that people.
And when he said, "Take your bow and quiver," he shows us that that people was disposed to love its own glory and not to be justified by faith,
but to trust in its own struggle and sword and to choose a rebellious king, as Moses said to them: "The sword is your boast."
And Rebecca said to her younger son: "Behold, I heard your father, for he was saying to Esau your brother:
'Hunt game for me and make me food, and I will eat and bless you before the Lord.'
Now, my child, listen to my words and go to the flock and bring me two young kids, and I will make food from them for him,
such as your father loves, and you shall bring it to your father, so that he may eat and bless you before his death."
Rebecca is said to be a figure of the Church, which showed forth beforehand, through that younger son, the things that were to come.
She said to him: "Go to the flock and bring me two young and beautiful kids."
He sends Esau to the field, as though revealing a life as a stranger within the kingdom, and Jacob to the flock, so that what was said by the Lord might be fulfilled:
"I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
And what he said to him, namely: "Bring me two kids, young and fine," shows us the two callings of the Gospel,
we who from the beginning were like kids, for all of us were under sin.
Now we become young and fine through obedience to Christ, justified by faith.
From now on we are not counted as kids, but as sheep we are offered as a fragrant, holy sacrifice to God, and through nourishment we are strengthened toward that spiritual word,
which in the Gospel he carried out in like manner toward the disciples, for he said to them: "I have food that you do not know."
And Jacob said to Rebecca his mother: "My brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man;
perhaps my father will touch me, and I shall be found before him as one who treats him with contempt, and I shall bring upon myself a curse and not a blessing."
Do you see that Jacob openly showed his fear, being aware of the deeds of Ham,
who saw the nakedness of Noah, his father, and laughed, for which he brought that curse upon himself?
Jacob too was afraid that he might be found to be one who put his father to the test, and be under a curse. And that saying of his was also true, namely:
"Esau my brother is hairy," which is said of one who is sinful, "and I am a smooth man," which shows the undefiled, spotless flesh of Christ.
But there was no other way by which that plan could be accomplished. She said to him: "Let that curse be upon me, son; only listen to me, and go and bring them to me."
And that saying of Rebecca, which is to be understood, is now fulfilled beforehand by the churches, and what she said, namely:
"Let that curse be upon me, son," signifies this to us: that now certain people reproach and despise the churches, and say:
We serve the Crucified One; this is the curse and contempt directed at us, for the sufferings of the Lord are a curse for unbelievers, but for believers they are life and peace.
For the Apostle too says: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, taking that curse upon himself for us."
As Christ has now accomplished: in his flesh he took upon himself death on the cross for the sake of human beings,
so that by his own humbling he might undo those curses of the Law which were upon Adam, for he said to him: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go."
And Rebecca took the precious, fine garment of her firstborn son and put it on Jacob her son, and she put the skins of the kid over his arms.
By the putting on of the garment he signifies to us the Word, who was prepared to put on flesh.
And the putting of the kid skins on his arms signifies to us the forgiveness of all sins through the stretching out of his hands upon the cross, as Isaiah says:
"He took our sins upon himself and bore our iniquities." And what Jacob said to his father:
"I have done as you commanded me" signifies to us the perpetual obedience of the Word to his Father, as Ezekiel says: "I have done what you commanded me."
And Isaac said to him: "Who are you?" And he said to him: "I am your firstborn son."
It was not out of ignorance that the prophet questioned Jacob, but because he was seeing the spiritual things that were to come.
Nor did Joshua son of Nun, who questioned the Gibeonites, know about them that evils were going to come from them through trickery,
but he knowingly let it pass, so that this people might believe in Joshua son of Nun and be saved.
So here too it must be understood, for he says: "Come near to me, that I may see you, my son, whether you are Esau, my son, or not."
And when he came near, he began to be troubled and said: "This voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are Esau's."
By this he indicates to us that the word addressed to Jacob reveals the counsel that was directed to the prophets, which he revealed beforehand through them concerning the things to come.
But his hands became like the hands of Esau, for he was given over to death because of the sins of the people,
And he said to him: "Come near and kiss me, son." And when he came near, he kissed him. And he smelled the scent of his garment and blessed him and said.
For this reason the prophet openly declares beforehand that no one among human beings shall kiss the Father
except only the Only-Begotten, the Son who was born of the virgin, for he says: "I am your firstborn son." And immediately, that which the Lord blessed [?].
And he said to him: "May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of wheat and wine, and may nations serve you,
and may rulers bow down to you, and be lord of your brother, and may the sons of your father bow down to you. Whoever blesses you,
may he be blessed, and whoever curses you, may he be cursed!" Now if anyone should think that these blessings were upon Jacob,
he is mistaken, for none of these things came about for Jacob, since he was found in Mesopotamia for twenty years as a slave of Laban.
And afterward he bowed down to his brother Esau and entreated his face with gifts, and after this he went down to Egypt, so that he and his offspring might not perish by famine.
Now upon whom is the saying fulfilled: "Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the scent of a full field, which the Lord has blessed"?
Not upon him, but upon Christ, the Son of God; the field is this world.
All who believe in him are in the fragrance of his coming, as the apostle says:
"We are the aroma of fragrance of Christ to the living and the dead: to some an aroma of death unto death, and to others an aroma of life unto life."
And as for what he said: "May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of wheat and wine,"
by this plain statement he indicates to us the Word, which came down from heaven like dew.
And in saying "of the fatness of the earth," he speaks of the flesh of the Lord, which was conceived of the virgin.
And in saying "an abundance of wheat and wine," he shows us the image of the saints, gathered into the storehouses and gladdened by the Spirit as if by wine.
And in saying: "May nations serve you and may authorities bow down to you," this is happening even up to the present time:
Whom do the believing nations serve to this day, and whom do rulers worship in the church, if not Christ, by whose name they are also saved?
As that word cries out through Isaiah: "Those who serve me, a new name shall be called upon them,
those who glorify me on earth, for they shall bless the true God, and those who swear by heaven shall swear by the living God."
And again he says: "Behold, those who serve me shall delight, but you shall hunger; behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, and you shall thirst.
Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame."
And immediately afterward he says: "Be lord of your brother, and the sons of your father shall worship you."
Yet no one worshipped Jacob, nor did he become lord of his brother Esau; for he came into conflict with Esau his brother, grew afraid and fled, and first bowed down before him seven times.
But now that saying is fulfilled in the Savior, for he whom one supposed to be his brother
was revealed in the flesh as lord over him, so that he might receive worship from them as king.
For this reason he says: "Whoever curses you, let him be cursed, and whoever blesses you, let him be blessed."
Now this blessing was spoken in word over Jacob, but in truth it is fulfilled in Christ.
Let us see what he says next, for he says: "And it came to pass after those blessings of Isaac upon Jacob,
and it came to pass, as Jacob was going out from Isaac his father, that Esau his brother also came with the game, and he made him food and brought it to his father."
Now he likens that food of Esau to the people who held to the service of the law, who boastfully supposed that they were justified by circumcision.
He sets forth the nations like that food, which goes outside [?] as a figure of the truth, and who did not dare to approach the heavenly bread. Esau said:
"Arise, my father, and eat of your son's game, and bless me with your soul."
Do you see the arrogance of his speech and the vehemence of his heart?
For even to this time those who are in circumcision boast in this way and suppose that they alone are justified.
But blessed Jacob came forward with fear and humility and said to his father: "I have done what you commanded me."
But Esau did not speak to him in this way, but vehemently: "Let my father arise and eat of this game, and bless me with your soul."
And he said: "Who are you?" And he said to him: "I am Esau, your firstborn son." Isaac grew faint with great astonishment and said:
"Then who was he who came before your coming and brought it to me, and I ate of everything and blessed him, and let him be blessed?"
Do you see how the prophet's spirit was awakened here?
For in the blessings to Jacob he spoke thus: "Whoever blesses you, let him be blessed, and whoever curses you, cursed."
For this reason he took care, and by that second statement he confirmed the earlier blessing, saying: "I blessed him, and let him be blessed."
And that counsel concerning Jacob was fulfilled in Christ, having been revealed beforehand: he who was blessed by the Father, begotten from the ages, was blessed forever.
But since the Scripture says, "Isaac marveled with great amazement," this means that he marveled at the things to come, which had been made known to him beforehand:
that the nations would be blessed through this child, this Son of God, and would enter into the promise together with the fathers.
For this reason also Jacob, at his birth, he who was to be born afterward, went forward and grasped the heel of Esau,
for that second people was prepared to follow in the footsteps of the prophets, to receive the birthright, and to appear as ruler in the new law.
And it came to pass, when Esau heard the word of Isaac his father, that he cried out with a loud voice, bitterly, and said: "Bless me also, father."
And Isaac said to him: "Your brother came with guile and took your blessing."
And when he said "with guile," he shows that it was done by design, for the Word of God was prepared to become incarnate and to put on the form of a servant,
so that through him, by an unrevealed birth, he might receive the blessing from the Father, and that it might be given to us also, who believe in him.
"And when Esau heard, he said: Rightly was his name called Jacob, for behold, twice he has deceived me: he took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing."
"And Esau threatened Jacob and said in his heart: May the days of my father's death draw near, so that I may kill Jacob my brother."
Thus the Scriptures here openly foretold, through Esau, the things that were to come, for the Word was being revealed as father of the people, he who afterward drew near to suffering in the flesh.
Moses also said reproachfully to the people: "Do you thus repay the Lord? Is not he himself your father?"
The Scripture has made this manifest so that we may understand what was said. And when Esau said:
"May the days of my father's death draw near," this refers to the day of fulfillment, when the word of the gospel concerning the kingdom was near to the fathers.
And when he says, "I will kill Jacob my brother," it is so that the man might be revealed who was born of Jacob according to the flesh, in likeness, and was hung by them on the tree.
And Esau said to him: "Have you not kept a blessing for me, father?" For there was complete silence of the Godhead, dwelling in like manner together with the flesh of Christ. And he said to him:
"If I have set him as lord over you and made all his brothers his servants, and have strengthened him with wheat and wine, what now shall I do for you, my son?"
"And Isaac was moved to pity. Esau raised a loud voice and wept." And when it says:

"Isaac was moved to pity," it signifies mercy, through that Word, for the sins of that people, for the Savior said to the Father in supplication: "Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."
And the loud voice and weeping of Esau show us repentance for the deeds they had done, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:
"When they heard this, they were grieved and said to Peter and the apostles: What shall we do, brothers?"
And they said to them: "Repent, believe in the name of Jesus Christ, and you will receive grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit,
For these promises are for you and for your children and for all who are far off, whom the Lord our God calls."
Now this is the blessing which Esau sought in the former time, but [he did not obtain it] because it was not yet the time.
But Isaac spoke prophetically about the things to come: "Behold, now your dwelling shall be from the fatness of the earth and from the dew of heaven above.
And by your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother. But it shall be that at some time you shall be set free and shall cast off his yoke from your neck."
Now, did that word of blessed Isaac have only the force of a blessing, or also that of a prophecy?
For we ought to understand it as concerning the things to come, for he said: "Behold, your dwelling shall be from the fatness of the earth, and from the dew of heaven above."
For the people's settlement was in that land of Ham, which Joshua the son of Nun apportioned to them; and as for what he said:
"From the dew of heaven": this is because the prophets, like dew from a cloud, let the word of God come down upon them.
And as for what he said: "By your sword you shall live":
this is because that people never ceased from warring and fighting against the surrounding nations among whom they had settled, as the books show us.
And what he said: "You shall serve your brother," he signified concerning these times, when Christ was near, in the visitation of his brethren,
who are so according to the flesh, and concerning whom the prophet teaches submission and servitude.
For this reason he said to him: "You shall be set free and shall cast off his yoke from your neck."
But what yoke, if not that of the law, which lay upon him, so that as slaves under the yoke they live by the law,
but as those set free they live by the faith of the gospel,
just as the blessed prophets from generation to generation proclaimed beforehand the counsel of Christ, and showed us openly what is right toward us.
Who, then, would doubt such manifest sayings? If they demand from us an account of things past and things to come, how much more should they have believed beforehand concerning what was to be?
Now the sayings of Isaac have been understood. Let us come also to the blessings of Jacob, those addressed to his sons.
For the Scripture speaks thus: "Jacob saw the sons of Joseph and said: Who are these?
And he said: They are my sons, whom the Lord has given me here. And he said: Bring them near to me, that I may bless them."
And Jacob's eyes were heavy with old age and he could not see, and he brought them near before him, and he put his hands around them and kissed them, and Israel said to Joseph:
"Behold, I have not been deprived of the sight of your face, and God has shown me your offspring as well."
And Joseph raised them from his bosom, and they bowed down with their faces to the ground.
And Joseph presented his two sons: Ephraim at his right, to Israel's left, and Manasseh at his left, to Israel's right. And he brought them near to him.
And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, and the left on the head of Manasseh, with his hands crossed one over the other.
He blessed them and said: "O God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac were pleasing, O God,
who have nurtured me from my youth until now, your angel, who delivered me from all my troubles, bless these boys,
and let my name be called upon them, and the name of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac, and let them multiply with great multiplication upon the earth."
When the prophet said this, he showed us a great counsel by crossing his hands one over the other, and by placing the younger son of Joseph,
Ephraim, on the right, and Manasseh, who was the firstborn, on the left.
Through them he shows us two callings and two peoples that were to be: the younger, found by faith at the right hand of Christ, while that first people,
who boasted in the Law, was placed on the left. For this reason Joseph could not understand what was to come from the prophet,
and he thought that his father had forgotten; for this reason he took hold of his hand and said to him: "Not so, father, for this one is the firstborn.
Place your right hand on his head." And he said to him: "I know, son, I know; this one too shall be great and shall be exalted.
But his younger brother shall be higher than he." And he set Ephraim above Manasseh. But indeed, what is unrevealed is great in the holy Scriptures.
So let us declare without grudging by what word the two sons of Joseph were made his own, for he said to him:
"These two children who were born to you in Egypt before I went down to Egypt shall be mine;
Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, like Reuben and Simeon. And the others from now on, as many children as you may have, shall be yours."
By this he indicates to us that the sons of Jacob were twelve, from whom came the twelve tribes; he made the two sons of Joseph into two tribes, and they became thirteen tribes.
He divided the tribe of Joseph between the two sons, and this was not for nothing,
for Paul the apostle was called the thirteenth, after the apostles; he was joined to the number of the tribes and was appointed apostle of the nations.
Now our minds have taken delight in the holy Scriptures, as proven by the prophets.
Let us see after this what he says, for it says: "Jacob called his sons and said to them: 'Gather around me and I will tell you
what is to happen to you in the latter times. Gather and listen, you sons of Jacob; listen to Israel, your father.'" And as for what he says, namely:
"Gather around me and I will tell you what is to happen to you in the times to come," this is prophecy and not blessing.
A blessing is spoken over someone when he is blessed, whereas a prophecy is made concerning the fulfilment of some matter.
And in the Scriptures it is said: "All these are the twelve sons of Jacob.
This their father said to them, and he blessed them, each according to his blessing."
And how could these things that are to be have unity, if at one time a prophecy is made manifest, or at another time the blessing is spoken?
By this we are given to understand that in the same words there are both blessings and prophecies,
So that the blessings might rest upon him who was born of Judah, who was made known to us through Joseph, and who came forth from Levi as priest of the Father.
But the prophecies are upon those who rose up to attack him and despised the Son of God.
If this is so, the Scriptures themselves teach us, for it says: "Reuben, my firstborn, you are the beginning and the strength of my children;
swiftly you grew up and swiftly you became arrogant. You have defiled like water. May you not boil over!
For you went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch onto which you went up."
Now what shall we say: is this a prophecy or a blessing?
And as for what he said: "Swiftly you grew up, and swiftly and arrogantly"; and as for what he said:
"You went up onto your father's bed, then you defiled the couch onto which you went up" — rather, it appears [?] to be a reproach, whether concerning deeds already done or concerning those to come.
Who knows, someone may say, that he said this because Reuben lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, for he defiled his father's bed.
Then, according to that word of his, it will be found that the prophet said one thing in place of another.
And in that word of his: "Gather together, you sons of Jacob, and I will tell you what is going to happen to you in the latter times,"
here the prophet is saying something about things to come. Now how then could we reckon it as concerning things already done?
Prophecy belongs to one who prophesies about things to come, and not about things already done.
And it is nothing great and nothing astonishing if something is visible among us two or three years beforehand, or if something else is told to others by prophecy.
And we may see with our eyes the things that have happened. Now let us show the prophet to be a prophet, for he says:
"Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my children."
And some apply this to the Savior, saying that the Father from above speaks these words to his Son.
But the words that follow become a cause of harm to readers and hearers.
And if anyone should suppose that it was said of Christ, where it says: "Swiftly you flourished
and swiftly became arrogant," he would also do harm to the rest of what is set down.
But it is not as they suppose: rather, he was the firstborn son of Jacob, and that people was firstborn, called through the Law a people of inheritance.
And he likened the deeds of Reuben, the firstborn, to the deeds that were to come from the first people.
And when he said: "Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my offspring," Jacob has authority [?] over Reuben; but when he said:
"Swiftly you grew up and swiftly became arrogant," he was seeing in the Spirit the disobedience and unbelief of his race.
For Moses too spoke to them in the same way: "You are a stiff-necked people. May the Lord not grow angry against you and wipe you out.
But as for what Jacob said, "You have defiled; like water may you not boil over," he cut short their fleshly standing,
for they defiled the Law and despised it, which was proclaimed to them through him and of which he said:
"You went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch onto which you went up."
By "bed" and "couch" he means that holy flesh in which the saints have come to rest as on a couch,
which the wicked in former times treated with contempt by holding out the vinegar and striking the head with the reed, as they struck his cheek with the hand and fastened his hands with nails.
All this was done to him by that disobedient and unbelieving people, and by the priests and the scribes, and by all the people together with their authorities.
For this reason the blessed prophet did not go along with [?] their deeds, nor did he share in their wicked counsels, but he separated himself from such crafty deeds of theirs.
For he says: "Simeon and Levi, brothers, carried out lawlessness by their conspiracy.
Let my soul not be united with their counsel, and let my inward being not share in their assembly, for in their anger they slew a man, and in their wrath they cut the sinews of a bull.
Cursed be their wrath, for it was in arrogance, and their anger, for it was in fierceness.
I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
And who knows this? Someone might suppose that blessed Jacob spoke that reproach of his two sons, Simeon and Levi, on account of the Shechemites,
because they deceitfully brought those Shechemites to submit to circumcision on account of Dinah, their sister, whom Hamor, the son of Shechem, had defiled.
They "went in after three days, slew all who dwelt in Shechem, and carried off their flocks as plunder."
But it was not so; rather, they themselves stated their reason to their father beforehand, namely that they had done justice.
Their father said to them: "You have made me hateful and an enemy to all who dwell in the land of the Canaanites and the Perizzites, and I am few in number.
They may gather against me and strike me and wipe out me and my people." And they answered and said to him: "And why did they treat our sister like a harlot?"
If this is so, they are to be praised for that deed and not blamed, they who showed such a manner of youth and were zealous for their sister, on account of the defilement by that son of Shechem.
And after this Jacob himself, in granting that city, said to blessed Joseph:
"I give you Shechem as my choice portion, above your brothers, which I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow and quiver."
If that is so, and Jacob himself justifies the slaughter of the Shechemites, where, then, is that prophecy fulfilled which says:
"Simeon and Levi carried out lawlessness by their unity. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my self not share in their assembly"?
Inquire of the Gospel and you will find the writings showing that those scribes were from the tribe of Simeon and those high priests from the tribe of Levi.
And since it was by their counsel and will that Christ was handed over, and by them that he was killed, the prophet knew it beforehand and spoke of their counsel.
What he speaks of here is that counsel which they were plotting against Christ, by which they killed him through treachery, as Isaiah says:
"Woe to them, for they have counseled an evil counsel against themselves, for they said: Let us bind the righteous one, for he has become troublesome to us."
"And let my soul have no share in their assembly," for at that time the high priests and the leaders of the people gathered against him;
they gathered in the house of the high priest Caiaphas to seek his death. "For in their wrath they slew men":
Which men, if not those blessed prophets who had been sent to them, and who were slain by them for preaching righteousness to them?
And "in their desire they cut the sinews of a bull."
He called their desire that of this world, for by the desire of this world they destroyed the heavenly leader of life, striking him down like a young bull.
For this reason he curses their anger, because it was with arrogance, and their wrath, because it was harsh.
By their anger he means the wrath in which they constantly lived, resisting the Holy Spirit with the stiffness of their necks.
"I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel." Who was Jacob, or who is Israel?
None other than the holy firstborn Son of God, to whom they did not submit, and so they were scattered to the ends of the heavens and were taken captive by enemies.
And since we said beforehand that the blessings are contained in what was spoken, it is better for lovers of learning to be persuaded, not by a demonstration in words only,
but also, with the full force of what was said, to make plain what lies before us; for he speaks to Judah in blessing thus: "Judah, your brothers will praise you.
Your hands will be on the shoulders of your enemies; the sons of your father will bow down to you.
A lion's whelp is Judah; from the shoot, my son, you have come forth. You went up, you lay down [?] like a lion and like a lion's whelp; who will rouse him?
A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a sovereign from his loins, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he will be the hope of the nations.
He will tie his ass to the vine, and to the tendril of the vine the foal of his ass. He has washed his adornment in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape.
His eyes are joyful as with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk."
How could this saying be like the one stated above, which was said about Reuben? For there he says to him:

"Harshly you would go, and harshly you became headstrong; you committed outrage like water; may you not boil over! For you went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch onto which you went up."
And what he said, namely: "Cursed be their anger, for it was with arrogance, and that wrath which was with harshness" — these words are not words of blessing but of reproach.
It was made manifest prophetically concerning them. And what he said, namely:
"Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hands will be on the shoulders of your enemies; the sons of your father will bow down to you" — words such as these resemble a blessing.
Who knows, [?] he said, by what word the prophet was made worthy of bestowing that blessing upon Judah, but not so upon those before him?
They learned that David was destined to be born from the tribe of Judah, and that Christ was destined to take on flesh from David.
He knew beforehand by the Spirit about those who were destined. He blessed David, who was from Judah, and the one who was to be born from him in the flesh, Christ,
so that he might not only receive that blessing spiritually from God, but might also appear blessed in the flesh, as Jeremiah says:
"Before you were formed in the womb I knew you, and before you had come forth from the womb I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations."
He who has come forth holy from the womb, by this God, is blessed. But you have said: Why did he not bless the tribe of Levi in this way?
For we have found Christ shown forth from the tribe of Levi as priest of the Father, because of the joining of that tribe of Levi with the company of Judah,
so that from those two he might appear as King and Priest and Son of God.
And Jacob looked upon the deed of the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, who dared to lay hands on that Son of God.
And because they were of the tribe of Levi, he did not bless Levi, but rather he coupled them together.
But when the blessed Moses came, he blessed Christ, who was born from Aaron and Levi, and said:
"Give to Levi his manifestation and his judgment, to the holy man." Thus, where the blessings from Jacob had fallen short, Moses came and completed them.
And now, on that account, let us speak about that blessing appointed for him. But now let us speak about what lies before us,
for it says: "Judah, your brothers shall bless you; your hands shall be upon the shoulders of your enemies; the sons of your father shall bow down to you."
Which brothers praised him and bowed down to him, if not the apostles, to whom the Lord said: "My brothers and fellow heirs"?
And as for what he said, "Your hands upon the shoulders of your enemies": it is because by the stretching out of his arms "he prevailed over those enemies,
he put those powers to shame," or else because, on account of the deeds done in the flesh, he became Lord and Judge over all, shown forth by the Father.
"Judah is a lion's whelp. From a sprouting, my child, you came forth." By saying "lion" and "lion's whelp" he has plainly shown us the twofold figure of the Father and of the Son.
And as for what he said, "From a sprouting you came forth, child," it is so that he might show us the birth of Christ through incarnation,

who sprang up from the womb of the Virgin through incarnation by the Holy Spirit, and came into the world like a flower and a fragrance and was revealed to us. And since "lion's whelp" was said of him,
as one born by the Father from the Holy Spirit, and as a King sent by a King,
he nevertheless did not remain silent on this account about what concerns the flesh, but said to him: "From a sprouting you came forth, child."
For Isaiah also says: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall spread out from it."
Now that root of Jesse was the lineage of the fathers, like a root planted on the earth, and the rod shown forth from them refers to Mary, for she was of the house and lineage of David.
And the flower that spread out from it is Christ, of whom Jacob said prophetically: "From a sprouting you came forth, child."
But as for what he said: "You went up, you [?] settled like a lion and like a lion's whelp."
He speaks of the three days' sleep, when he remained in the heart of the earth, to which the Lord himself testified, saying:
"As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so also must the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights."
And David says beforehand: "I lay down, I slept, I awoke, for the Lord was my helper." So also Jacob says: "Who shall raise him up?"
And he did not say, "No one shall raise him up," but he said "who," for this is to be understood of "the Father, who raised his Son from the dead."
And Peter says: "Whom God raised up, having loosed the bonds of hell, for it was not possible that he should be held by it."
And again he truly shows us his birth according to the flesh, for he says:
"A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it has been prepared, and he shall be the hope of the nations."
And indeed neither authority nor a leader failed from the tribe of Judah until the coming of Christ.
And in the Gospel it likewise testifies. And when the Savior came, he became the hope of the nations,
who to this very day have believed in him. And this is manifest, for whom do we await from heaven for our salvation?
None other than him for whom the law and the prophecies have been prepared.
And again he says: "He shall bind his foal to the vine, and to the tendril of the vine, the colt of the ass." He foretells to us both of the callings to him,
bound as to a vine and united with one another by his love, the foal and the colt loosed together by a word, on which the Savior sat and entered Jerusalem.
And again he begins and says: "He washed his adornment with wine."
And here, in a veiled way, he foretells to us baptism, when, coming up from the Jordan, he sanctified the waters and spread over them the graces of the Holy Spirit.
By adornment he meant the flesh, and by wine the paternal Spirit, who descended upon him at the Jordan. "And with the blood of the grape his garment."
By the word "garment" he foretells to us the nation, those who are counted as garments to him.
Through the prophet he says: "As I live, says the Lord, surely all of them shall be put on like garments."
And indeed he was the grape and the cluster that was hung upon the wood, from whom, when they pierced his side,
blood and water poured down, for some as baptism and for others as ransom. Concerning these the prophet said:
"He washed his adornment with wine and his garment with the blood of the grape." Only then are they revealed to his prophets and apostles:
"His eyes are joyful as with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk."
The eyes of Christ were the prophets, gladdened by the power of the Spirit, who proclaimed beforehand concerning his sufferings,
and who related them to later generations, so that people who believe in him might be saved.
And as for what he said, "His teeth are white as milk," he is speaking of the apostles,
who by that same word were shown to be purified like milk, and who also poured out upon us that spiritual grace and heavenly food.

And further he is speaking of the service of the Lord, those who, having come forth from that holy mouth, became milk for us, so that, nourished by them, we may be made worthy to share also in that heavenly mouth.
And further he says: "Zebulun shall dwell by the seashore, and he shall be a harbor for sailors, and he shall extend as far as Sidon."
Now by Zebulun, who is set forth here, he designates the nations, who now dwell in this world as on a seashore and are tossed about by waves as in a sea,
and who flee and take refuge in the Church as in a harbor. He speaks of a resting place for ships, meaning the cities with the assemblies of the Church,
which are spread out in this world like harbors and are a refuge for believers who turn to it, as the prophet says:
"Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way by the sea, beyond the Jordan!
The people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and on those who sat in the shadows of death a light has shone." He is speaking of the faith of the people.
And as for what he said, "He shall reach as far as Sidon," he reveals the long-suffering of God, who showed long-suffering even to the very last of them.
And the nations who now believe shall be saved. For Sidon was the first-born offspring of Ham.
And Ham, because of his sins against his father, was under the curse; and his race has come to believe and is now blessed by Christ.
"Issachar desired what is good. He rests among the portions, and he saw the rest, that it is good, and the land, that it is rich; he gave his shoulders to labor and became a man who works the land."
And Issachar in a spiritual sense is likened to the Lord, who from childhood was eager only for what is good.
As Isaiah says: "Before the child yet knows how to call out the name of father or mother, he will not submit to evil, but will choose the good."
He rests among the portion of the prophets, so that what was spoken by them might be fulfilled.
For on the mountain Moses and Elijah appeared, standing on the right and on the left and speaking with him, and the Savior was shown as one at rest.
Now he saw the rest of the saints, that it is good, and their land, that it is rich; "he gave his shoulders to labor and became a man who works the land."
Where then did he give his shoulders to labor, if not to the cross, which he took up and carried?
And Isaiah says: "He who had dominion upon his shoulders." This one stretched out his hands upon the crossbeam and took the labor upon himself, that is, the reproach and insult that were upon him.
He became a man of the Church by gathering good fruit in it.
"Dan shall judge his people, as one tribe of Israel. And Dan shall be like a serpent lying in ambush on the road, to strike the heels of the horse.
The riders shall fall backward, waiting for the salvation of the Lord." For he says: "Dan shall judge his people, as one tribe of Israel."
And this one portion was about Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan. He judged his people for only twenty years.
But it is wholly fulfilled with regard to the usurper, who, as a wicked judge and a usurper born as king, will judge his people, as a usurper,
"like a serpent lying in ambush on the road," and who will begin to bite, in opposition to the word of truth, those who walk rightly.
But as for what the prophet says, "to strike the heels of the horses," he will reach out against those who teach us the righteous way, the way of life.
Just as he tested the apostles and enticed Judas, and threw him down like a horse and gave over to death the one sitting on it, and as the horseman fell backward,
that is, from the last ones to the former ones, by the waiting for the Lord's salvation he raised up and set upright the image of Adam.
"Gad: with a testing it shall test him, and he too shall test them." He readily calls a testing that wicked assembly of the chief priests and scribes,
who were testing the Savior with various temptations, wanting to find some pretext against him, so that they might seize him by guile and kill him.
But he knew their thoughts and at once put them to the test by his justice, and through their sin they gave him over to death.
As it is written in the Gospel: at that time the Pharisees stood before him and said to him:
"Teacher, tell us, by what authority do you do this, or who gave you this authority?"
And he said to them: "I too will ask you one thing; tell me, and I too will tell you by what authority I do this: the baptism of John, where was it from?
Was it from heaven, or from men?" And they reasoned in their hearts and said: "If we say to him, 'It was from heaven,' he will say to us, 'Then why did you not believe him?'
And if we say, 'From men,' all the people will stone us," for all knew of John that he was a great prophet.
They answered and said to him: "We do not know." And he said: "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do this."
Now the prophet says well: "Gad: it shall test him, and he too shall test them."
"Asher: his bread is richness, and he shall nourish rulers."
Here the prophet makes known to us concerning the apostles, who took care and gave the bread of life to the race of men; this he shows us concerning Christ.
That bread which came down from heaven became bread for food and drink for the saints.
For Asher is translated "wealth," meaning the one who alone is rich and powerful for all, for the Lord himself testifies concerning himself and says: "I am the bread that came down from heaven.
The fathers ate the manna in the desert and perished, but whoever eats my bread will not see death forever."
We must inquire into this as well, for he does not say that he will not die, but he says:
"He will not see death forever," and forever and ever by the torment of fire, which is eternal death, which never subsides.
For the life of these times is this passing world, and death is due to all men.
If this is so, the Lord is not speaking of the death of these times, but of those that have been prepared.
"Naphtali: sprung up and flourishing and firmly rooted, made beautiful."
"A sprouted shoot": by this he signifies to us those peoples who, freed by faith, were called, through whom we all are made able.
In the divine sense he calls Christ a spiritual vineyard.
The branch and shoot are the saints who believe in him, and the cluster is the martyrs, and the wood tied to the vine signifies to us their sufferings.

And he speaks of the grape-gatherers, meaning the angels; and the basket into which they gather the fruit of the vineyard is the apostles, the winepress is the church, and the wine is the power of the Holy Spirit.
And as for what he said, "a sprouted shoot," it means freed from the bonds of death, as Isaiah
says: "Let them go out and leap like calves let loose from a rope."
"Let them grow, adorned and firmly rooted": for by that birth from above, by water, they obtain the beauty of the Word, who is "fairer than all the sons of men."
"My son, flourishing Joseph. My blessed son, my envied son, my young plant, return to me!"
Those men, archers, who plotted against you and held envy toward you: their bows were shattered with might, and the sinews of their arms were loosed by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob.
By this Israel was strengthened by the God of your father, and my God helped you and blessed you with the blessing of heaven and with blessing upon the earth,
who held the earth for the sake of the blessings of your mother's breasts and of the womb of your father and your mother.
Be stronger than the eternal mountains, and more desirable than the eternal hills! Let it rest upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the head, by which he led his brothers.
And he blessed Joseph above his brothers, for through him it was portrayed and made visible that the plots against Christ were carried out.
For this reason also the prophet spoke with a blessing not upon Joseph, but upon the one whose figure he displayed, for he said to him: "My flourishing son Joseph."
For he flourished by the Spirit perfected by the Lord. Upon the earth the graces of Christ were multiplied.
"My blessed and envied son": for he was blessed by God; he came to his own and they did not know him, but they grew envious and hated him, for the scripture says:
"His brothers saw that he was beloved of his father, and they envied him and hated him." Therefore Jacob says: "My envied son, my youthful son."
And again it says: "Jacob loved him, because he was to him a son of his old age."
Now to this aged and utterly perishing world the Son of God appeared, and he was born of a virgin.
An aged Son he appeared from the Father, he who was with the Father before the ages.
Therefore he says to him: "Return to me, son," as if calling his own son from earth to heaven,
"about whom the archers plotted and were envious." Who were they who plotted a plot of wickedness and reproached him?
It was that lawless and disobedient people, who greatly and [?] reproached him.
"Men who were archers": for it seemed easy to them to do evil to all those righteous ones and to kill them.
And their bows were shattered with might, for however much evil they spoke about him, as if drawing it up on the bow, afterwards they themselves were put to shame,
When they perceived concerning him that he had risen from the dead, as Isaiah says: "Vain are the counsels for your souls."
And Jacob says: "The sinews of their arms were loosed by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob."
They who had nothing for themselves and no hope toward God, and who boasted in their own strength,
became as though they had never been, trampled down by his word and scattered by him among the nations.
"Israel, who was strengthened by the God of your father, and my God helped you."
Who is it that strengthened Israel and helped his servant, if not God alone? As he says through the mouth of Isaiah:
"Jacob, my servant, I have helped you; and Israel, my chosen one, my soul has accepted him."
And again he says: "Do not fear, be strong, and do not be ashamed, for they [?]."
Because of the insult and reproach that were spoken against him, he spread out that blessing and said:
"I have blessed you with the blessing from above and the blessing of the earth, which holds all [?]." He subjected all things under his feet.
"From heaven above" means the blessing of heaven, and "of the earth" means the blessing of the earth, so that he might be shown to be Lord over angels and human beings,
he who was despised by them. "And for the blessings of the breasts and of the womb of your mother, the blessing of your father and of your mother."
He speaks of the blessing of the breasts either with reference to the two laws, through which the Word was proclaimed so that he might be made manifest to the world,
and through which he also delights us as with milk, nourishes us, and presents us as children of God;
or else he indicates to us the breasts of holy Mary, by which he was nourished, which were blessed, and concerning which the woman cried out to him, saying:
"Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you."
And as for what he added, saying: "Blessed is the womb of your father and of your mother,"
the prophet shows beforehand a spiritual meaning, for he could have said, "and blessed is the womb of your mother,"
so as to point by this mention to Mary, in whose womb the Word was nourished.
But he did not say this; rather, he says: "Blessed is the womb of your father and of your mother."
By joining both together he presented them as one, so that they might understand concerning him both spiritually and bodily,
for he was the Word of the Father and from a holy womb, as one born from the womb of the Father.
As the prophet says: "My heart has uttered a good word." In like manner he is also, in the flesh, born of the Virgin,
so that he might be shown to be born from the womb of a mother, as the prophet said: "Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant."
And through the mouth of Jeremiah he says: "Before knowing you, I knew you beforehand in the womb, and before your coming forth from the womb, I loved you."
For the Word was born both spiritually and in the flesh, and appeared as God and as man in very truth; rightly, then, did the prophet speak of the womb of mother and father.
If someone does not understand it in this way, the prophet may seem laughable to some, for it is fitting to speak of a womb only in the case of a woman.
But here he says, "the blessed womb of your mother and father," so that you may understand that the Word was born in two ways, from God and from the virgin, and on account of this he goes on to say:
"He has grown strong with blessing above the everlasting mountains and is more desirable than the eternal hills."
He grew strong above the patriarchs and above the apostles and prophets, being exalted by God.
He gathered all those blessings upon his head, for "the head of all the saints is Christ."
And so he says: "They rested upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of him who led his brothers."
When he said "his brothers," he did not say it of those who were his brothers according to the flesh, for he rejected them,
but he said it of those who were reckoned as brothers spiritually, of whom the Lord said: "My brothers and fellow heirs."
It was of such as these that Jacob spoke, spreading that blessing over those whom Christ himself reckoned as his brothers.
"Benjamin is a ravening wolf; at dawn he will eat food, and toward evening he will divide provisions among rulers."
"A ravening wolf" clearly points to Paul, who was born of the tribe of Benjamin.
A ravening wolf, who formerly tore apart and devoured the lambs of the Church, as Paul himself confesses, saying:
"I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I greatly persecuted the churches of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am."
For this reason too Rachel gave his birth the name "son of my pain, Benjamin."
She spoke prophetically of the things to come, for Paul, born of the tribe of Benjamin, would distress and afflict,
as if his own mother, that is, the Church herself, by killing all who called on the name of God.
From the beginning he was a blasphemer and a reviler; afterward he repented and spread out to all that spiritual and heavenly food, first distributing Christ among the nations,
to whom let us too give thanks in faith for ever and ever. Amen.
